study: Learn the definition: NLP is a branch of AI that focuses on interaction between computers and humans, with Alexa, Siri and ChatGPT as examples.
Draw the generic NLP system as one line: input, Automatic Speech Recognition, NLU, NLG, output, with one line on each block.
Memorise the five stages in order: lexical or morphological, syntactic, semantic, discourse integration, pragmatic, each with its one-line job.

Learn one teacher example per stage: The cat is running (tokens), The dog chased the ball (order), The apple ate the boy (meaning), John wants to read a book. He picked it up (discourse), It's freezing out here (pragmatic).
Copy the five-row table: stage, question it answers, example. It doubles as the full answer for a 5-mark question.
tricks: The five stage names plus one example each are the skeleton for the stages questions, and the same five levels reappear in the ambiguity types (lexical, syntactic, semantic, anaphoric, pragmatic) and in the challenges table, so learn them once.
The process diagram (input, ASR, NLU, NLG, output) is the only extra block needed for 'also explain generic NLP system'; draw it first, then the stages.
The 'apple ate the boy' versus 'chased ball the dog' pair is a ready one-line example of why syntax and semantics are different stages; reuse it in any ambiguity or challenges answer.
John wants to read a book. He picked it up is the same sentence used for anaphora resolution in the discourse topic, so one example serves both.

study: Learn the definition: ambiguity is a word, sentence or phrase with multiple meanings, with the teacher's example I saw a man with telescope.

Memorise the five types with one example each: lexical (bank), syntactic (I saw a man with telescope), semantic (someone ate every slice of pizza), anaphoric (Mary told Susan that she had won), pragmatic (Do you know the time?).
Copy the syntactic versus lexical comparison table: definition, source, focus, example, resolution (parsing against WSD), relevance in NLP.
Learn the remedy for each type: WSD, parsing, meaning and context, pronoun resolution (Hobbs, Centering), context and speaker intention.

Learn the stage-by-challenge table and the applications table of nine rows: machine translation, IR, QA, text classification, summarization, sentiment analysis, NER, language models, speech assistants.
tricks: The five-type list with one example each answers the ambiguity-types question, the 'ambiguity at each level' question and the challenges question, because the challenges table is the same five types tied to stages.

The syntactic versus lexical table is a ready 5-mark answer; its two rows 'resolution: parsing' and 'resolution: WSD' also point you to the cfg-parsing and word-sense-disambiguation topics, so quote them there too.

The applications table (nine one-line rows) answers every 'applications of NLP' question and can be shortened to three or four rows for a 5-marker; the same applications are explained in full in the NLP applications topic.
Answer skeleton for 'ambiguity, types and ways to resolve': definition, tree diagram of the five types, one example each, then one resolution line per type.

study: Learn the definition: data preprocessing is cleaning a text before giving it to computers, with the Hello bbbb, we all love NL@P example.
Memorise the seven steps in order: extraction and noise removal, tokenization, case normalization, stop-word removal, term normalization, stemming or lemmatization, feature extraction and indexing.
Learn the one-sentence pipeline: The Cats are Running in the Garden! becomes cats, running, garden, and then cat, run, garden after stemming.
Learn stemming against lemmatization: retrieval, retrieved, retrieving become retriev; better becomes good, mice becomes mouse.
Learn regular expression: a pattern to match and replace text, with its four jobs (tokenization, text cleaning, pattern matching, information extraction) and the teacher's example for each.
tricks: The seven-step pipeline with the Cats and Garden example is the same list asked as 'text processing steps for Information Retrieval' in the NLP applications topic, so one learning gives both answers.
Tokenization and stemming (5 marks) needs only two rows from this note: tokenization breaks text into tokens, and the retriev example; reuse the retriev example in the Porter stemmer answer.
The regex four-jobs table is the full answer to 'significance of regular expression'; add the three example patterns [0-9]+, <[^>]+> and \w+ if you want extra marks.
Any 'explain preprocessing' 10-marker: definition, seven-block flow diagram, a table of step and detail, then the worked sentence.

study: Learn the definition: stemming finds the root word; the Porter stemmer is a rule-based algorithm with 5 sets of rules, fast and simple, by Martin Porter, and it helps IR.
Learn the consonant and vowel rule (y is a vowel after a consonant) and the form [C](VC)^m[V], with the three steps to find m.
Memorise the measure examples: TREE 0, TROUBLE 1, TRAP 1, TROUBLES 2, PRIVATE 2, RELATIONAL 4.
Learn the rule form (condition) S1 to S2 with the example (m > 1) EMENT to nothing, so REPLACEMENT becomes REPLAC.
Memorise the five-step table: 1a plurals, 1b -ed and -ing, 1c y to i, 2 and 3 long suffixes, 4 remove suffixes, 5 final e and double l.
Practise the three traces: generalizations to gener, relational to relat, hopefulness to hope.
tricks: This one answer is asked in 7 papers, so learn it as a block: definition, flow diagram of the five steps, measure, rule form, steps table, one trace. The same block answers 'illustrate with example' and 'with rules' variants.
Pick the trace by what the question gives: generalizations if it asks for a long word, relational if it asks for m = 4, hopefulness if it asks why a final e stays.
The retriev and connect examples link this topic to text preprocessing and to IR text processing, so a one-line mention there earns marks cheaply.
The 'limits' bullets (happi is not a word, universe and university both become univers) double as the stemming against lemmatization comparison.

study: Learn morphology as stem plus affixes (prefix, infix, suffix), with the examples unsuccessful, unfriendly, undoable and deciphered, and the small FSA drawn as q0 to q3.
Learn the affix definition (a bound morpheme added to a stem to change its meaning or function) and the three types with one example each.
Copy the inflectional against derivational table: same word in a new form (school to schools) against a new word (paint to painter).
Learn the FSA five parts (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F) and the five points of the role of FSA in morphological analysis, with the cats example.
Memorise the four-row output table: walked is walk + V + Past, went is go + V + Past, cat is cat + N + Sg, cats is cat + N + Pl.
Draw the FST for regular and plural nouns with arcs cat:cat, epsilon:+N, epsilon:+Sg and s:+Pl, and the FSA for numbers 1 to 99.
tricks: The four-row output table answers 'output of morphological analysis' and also supplies the examples for the FST role answer; draw the cats FST right after it.
The same q0 to q3 prefix, stem, suffix FSA answers 'explain FSA for nouns and verbs' and 'role of FSA in morphological analysis'; only the labels change.
Derivational examples (success to successful, friend to friendly, install to installment) come from the FSA drawings, so one example list serves both the FSA and the derivational answers.
Any 'design an FST or FSA' question: write the tuple, draw states with labelled arcs, mark the final state with a double circle, then trace one accepted and one rejected word.

study: Learn the language model definition (predicts the next word, gives probabilities to sequences) and the N-gram definition, with unigram, bigram and trigram and the I want to drink example.
Memorise the bigram formula P(B given A) = count(AB) / count(A) and the five-step method: add start and end symbols, count unigrams, count bigrams, divide, pick the highest.
Practise the Sam corpus: after like the answer is college (0.6), after Sam the answer is the end symbol (0.6).
Practise the I tell you to sleep corpus: after to the answer is sleep (2/3), relax is 1/3.
Learn smoothing (add-one, add-k, Good-Turing, Kneser-Ney), perplexity (lower is better, 1 is perfect) and the five spelling correction steps with skul to school.
tricks: The bigram table method (count pairs, divide by the first word's count) answers every corpus numerical: Sam, sleep and the four students corpus; only the counting changes, and the check that probabilities after one word add to 1 catches mistakes.

The same bigram counts feed the sentence comparison question: multiply the bigram probabilities from start to end and the larger product wins; a zero count makes the product 0, which leads into the smoothing answer.
The language model definition and 'She went to the' probabilities are the same block used in the NLP applications topic (language models), so it is one learning for two topics.
The N-gram note also answers the spelling correction, text prediction and 'N-gram and its application' questions; use the uses list as the applications part.

study: Learn the definition: POS tagging assigns each word a grammatical category, with The quick brown fox example tagged DT JJ JJ NN VBZ IN DT JJ NN.

Learn open class (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs: content words, new words added) against closed class (pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions, determiners: function words) with the comparison table.
Memorise the tagged sentence He/PRP used/VBD to/TO provide/VB help/NN to/IN other/JJ people/NNS.
Learn the three kinds of taggers: rule-based (the -tion or -ment gives noun rule), stochastic (HMM, MaxEnt), hybrid (statistics first, rules correct).
Memorise the four challenges: ambiguity (book as noun or verb), idioms, out-of-vocabulary words, domain dependence.
tricks: The open and closed class table with four examples each answers the open or closed class question, the types of word classes question and the first half of the tagging sentence question.
Ambiguity of book (noun and verb) is the same example used in the ambiguity topic and the WSD idea, so one example serves the challenges answer here and there.
The rule-based against stochastic table answers 'what is rule-based and stochastic tagger' and sets up hybrid tagging as the combination; learn it together with the HMM note's limitations.
The challenges list (ambiguity, idioms, OOV, domain) overlaps with HMM limitations (unseen words) and NLP challenges, so reuse the out-of-vocabulary line.

study: Learn the HMM definition, its five components (states, observations, transition, emission, initial probabilities) and the diagram of hidden states with emissions to observations.
Memorise the two counting formulas P(t_j given t_i) = Count(t_i to t_j) / Count(t_i) and P(word given tag) = Count(word, tag) / Count(tag), then the Viterbi steps.
Practise the Justin will spot Will example: the path up to spot is NNP, MD, VB with probability 0.0247, using start 1/9.
Learn the ten limitations of HMM (independence assumption, limited context, fixed states, sparsity, unseen words and so on) and the two limitations of MaxEnt (label bias, computation cost).
Learn MaxEnt: discriminative, P(y given x) with feature functions, weights and Z(x), the feature type table, and the made-up run after TO example giving VB 0.924.
Learn CRF: global normalization over the whole sequence, no label bias, and the HMM, MaxEnt, CRF comparison table.
tricks: The count-then-multiply Viterbi method on a tagged corpus answers all the HMM numericals in the exam (the corpus table and the 'consider the following corpus' questions); only the corpus changes, so practise the Justin example once.
The 10-point HMM limitations list is asked 4 times; the MaxEnt limitations and CRF's global normalization answer the 'compare HMM, MaxEnt, CRF' angle using the three-column table.

The formula block for MaxEnt, with the lambda weights and Z(x), is the whole answer to 'explain MaxEnt for POS tagging' and 'MaxEnt for sequence labelling': definition, feature table, formula, limitations.
The CRF line (probabilistic model that understands sequence and context) also appears in NER methods in the NLP applications topic, so reuse it there.

study: Learn the class grammar by heart: S to NP VP, NP to Det N or N, VP to V NP, Det to The or this, N to man or book, V to read, with the sentence The man read this book.
Learn the top-down against bottom-up table (leftmost derivation against reduction to S) and the two derivations of The man read this book.
Learn the shift-reduce parts (stack, input buffer, shift, reduce, accept, error) and the 15-step trace, plus the conflict at step 5.
Learn the CYK steps (CNF, diagonal, spans of length 2 to n with split points, S in the top cell) and the filled table where the final cell holds S.
Learn PCFG (rule probabilities, product for a tree, choose the highest) and the three CFG problems with fixes: agreement, subcategorization, movement.
tricks: One grammar and one sentence (The man read this book) drives four answers: the derivation, the parse tree, the shift-reduce trace and the CYK table; learn the grammar once and reuse it for all of them.
The final tree [S [NP [Det The] [N man]] [VP [V read] [NP [Det this] [N book]]]] is the parse tree answer for CYK and also the result of the shift-reduce parse; draw it at the end of both.
Top-down against bottom-up is a ready table with an example pair of derivations, and shift-reduce is its bottom-up example, so quote the table in the shift-reduce answer's introduction.
The I saw the man with the telescope ambiguity (from the ambiguity topic) is the example for PCFG too: two trees, pick the more probable.

study: Learn lexeme (a word or phrase with a specific meaning) and lexicon (all lexemes of a language), with content words against function words and the cat example.
Memorise the seven relations in order: homonymy, polysemy, synonymy, antonymy, hypernymy, hyponymy, meronymy, plus holonymy as the reverse of meronymy.
Learn one example per relation: bank and bank, head, smart and intelligent, hot and cold, animal and dog, dog and animal, wheel and car.
Learn the three antonym kinds: gradable (hot, cold), complementary (alive, dead), relational (buy, sell).
Learn the lexical analysis of I deposited money in the bank: find lexemes, look up meanings, bank is homonymy, context words choose the financial sense.
tricks: The seven-row relations table with one example each answers the full relations question, and any four-relation question (homonymy to antonymy, or hyponymy to holonymy) just uses part of the same table.
The I deposited money in the bank example is the answer to 'lexical semantic analysis with an example' and the same sentence is the Lesk worked example in the WSD topic, so learn it once.
The animal, dog, cat, elephant tree answers hypernymy, hyponymy and, with wheel and car added, meronymy and holonymy, in one diagram.
The semantic analysis answer needs only the five-block flow: sentence, lexemes, relations, word sense disambiguation, meaning of the sentence.

study: Learn the WSD definition (choosing the correct meaning of a word with several senses from context), the bank deposit and river bank examples, and the four approaches diagram.
Learn the dictionary-based approach: compare context words with the definitions of each sense, count the overlap, take the maximum.
Learn Lesk's five steps (select word, context window, compare definitions, count overlaps ignoring the, a, and, choose the highest) and the bank worked example.
Learn Lesk advantages (simple, no training) and disadvantages (low accuracy for similar senses, low recall, dictionary dependent).
Learn Yarowsky: seeds, decision list, confident labels, one sense per collocation, one sense per discourse, iterate until no new labels.
Learn supervised Naive Bayes (argmax of P(s) times the product of P(c_j given s)) and Hyperlex (hubs of a word graph) for the 4-way comparison table.
tricks: The Lesk bank overlap count (sense 1 gets money, so 1; sense 2 gets 0) answers the dictionary-based approach question, because Lesk is that approach; so one learning covers 'dictionary-based approach' (5 papers) and 'Lesk' (3 papers).

The four-row table (knowledge-based, supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised: Lesk, Naive Bayes, Yarowsky, Hyperlex) is the skeleton for any 'WSD approaches' question and for the Yarowsky and Hyperlex question.
For the need of WSD, say that a word with several senses causes lexical ambiguity and WSD finds the intended sense from the context; the ambiguity topic uses the same line.
The same bank sentence appears in lexical semantics and ambiguity answers, so any WSD answer can start with the two bank senses.

study: Learn discourse analysis (connect sentences so the meaning stays coherent) with its four points and Taylor went to the store. She bought groceries.
Learn pragmatic analysis (intended meaning beyond the literal) with its examples: Can you pass the salt?, I'm falling for you, and the table against discourse.
Learn reference resolution: referring expression, referent, antecedent, and Ram laughed as loud as he could with the five-step flow.
Memorise the five referring expressions: indefinite NP, definite NP, pronoun, demonstrative, name, each with the class example.
Learn the extra topics: anaphora against cataphora, the three complicating referents (inferrables, discontinuous sets, generics), and the agreement constraints (number, person, case, gender).
tricks: The five-row referring expressions table is both its own question and the first half of any 'reference resolution in detail' answer; follow it with the Ram laughed flow and the constraints.

Discourse against pragmatic uses the same table as the last two stages in the NLP introduction topic and the anaphoric and pragmatic ambiguity types, so the Taylor and Can you pass the salt examples work there too.
Answer skeleton for 'reference resolution in detail' (asked 4 times): definition, example, five types, difficulties (three referents), constraints, then name Hobbs and Centering from the next topic.
The agreement constraint example 'The chefs made lunch. She served it' is a ready one-line illustration for number agreement, and the same match rule is the gender and number check in Hobbs.

study: Learn the Hobbs definition (heuristic by Jerry Hobbs, 1976, works on the syntactic tree) and its four steps: start at the pronoun and go up, collect nouns, apply gender, number and distance, repeat if none.
Practise the Hobbs example John saw Mary, he greeted her: Mary rejected for gender, he is John, her is Mary.
Learn the Centering definition and its terms: Cf (ranked entities), Cp (preferred centre, the subject), Cb (centre carried over), and the five steps.
Learn the three transitions in order of preference: Continue, Retain, Shift, with the Aragorn and Frodo example.
Copy the Hobbs against Centering table: syntactic tree against discourse focus, one pronoun against whole text, gender, number and distance against centre continuity.
tricks: The Hobbs against Centering table is the whole answer to the 'compare' question and also the skeleton for 'how anaphora resolution is performed with both'; write one definition each, then the table.
The Aragorn and Frodo sentences give a Continue, Retain and Shift answer in three lines; reuse this working in any Centering numerical or example.
John saw Mary, he greeted her is the shortest complete worked example; the gender and number constraints it uses are the same agreement constraints from the discourse and reference topic.
Centering's applications (machine translation, summarization, story generation, conversational AI) link to the NLP applications topic and fill out the importance section cheaply.

study: Learn machine translation: definition, the six-step working (input, preprocessing, encoding, translation, decoding, output), and the three methods rule-based, statistical (parallel corpora, IBM models) and neural (encoder-decoder, attention, Transformer).
Learn MT evaluation (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, human) and the advantages against limitations table.
Learn information retrieval: definition, the smart librarian analogy, user side, system side (inverted index, matching, RSV), and the seven text processing steps; then the IR against IE table.
Learn question answering: question analysis, IR, answer extraction, plus extractive against generative and open against closed domain.
Learn summarization (extractive with TextRank against abstractive) and NER (definition, entity types, six working steps, four methods including CRF).
Also revise text classification, sentiment analysis (five types, four approaches) and language models (statistical n-gram, neural RNN, LSTM, Transformer) for the short-note questions.
tricks: The three-method MT diagram (rule-based, statistical, neural) answers 'MT in detail', 'MT approaches', 'rule-based MT' and 'statistical MT' by writing the full diagram or just the one box; this block is asked 4 times plus 3 smaller variants.
The seven-step IR text processing list is the same as the preprocessing topic's pipeline, so learning one gives both answers, and the Cats and Garden example fits either.
IR against IE is a ready 5-row table; use NER as the bridge (NER is an IE step), and use the table with the IR definition for 'compare IR and IE' asked 4 times.
Any 'explain X system in detail' 10-marker here: definition, pipeline flow diagram, methods or types table, evaluation or advantages against limitations, applications.
